title: Jummah Masjid
address: Royal Road, Queen St, Port Louis, Mauritius
about_site_text: Port Louis's principal mosque, on Royal Road in the heart of the old commercial quarter. Members of the city's mercantile community bought the site on Queen Street in 1852 and consecrated the mosque in 1853, when it was known as the "Mosque of the Arabs." A major expansion begun in 1878, overseen by Jackaria Jan Mahomed, was delayed for years by disease and construction-supply shortages and wasn't finished until 1895 - the building seen today is largely that late-19th-century enlargement.
interesting_fact: The mosque blends Indian, Creole and Islamic architectural styles, and is widely described as one of the most beautiful religious buildings in Mauritius. A marble tomb beside the mosque holds the remains of Jamal Shah, a pir (Sufi holy man) from Kutch in India.

title: Government House
about_site_text: The seat of Mauritius's colonial and now national government, at the top of Place d'Armes. The first Government House, built of wood in 1725 under the French, was destroyed by a cyclone in 1727. Construction of a permanent building began under French governors Nicolas de Maupin and Mahé de Labourdonnais, who enlarged it into the building's current footprint in 1738, originally named the Hôtel du Gouvernement.
interesting_fact: Place d'Armes, the grand palm-lined boulevard leading up to it, is often called the most iconic street in Mauritius and is lined with statues of figures from the island's history.

title: Place d'Armes
about_site_text: The grand royal-palm-lined boulevard running from Government House down to the waterfront, and the most iconic public space in Port Louis. Originally the site of a fortification and battery built by Governor De Nyon and later reinforced by Mahe de Labourdonnais, it was laid out as the ceremonial approach to Government House, the French colonial residence dating to 1738. Today the avenue is lined with statues of the figures who shaped the island's history, from colonial governors like Sir William Stevenson and Sir John Pope Hennessy to Queen Victoria and lawyer Sir William Newton, who helped democratise Mauritius's electoral system.
interesting_fact: At the quayside end of the avenue stands a bronze statue of Mahe de Labourdonnais, cast by French sculptor A. Dumont and inaugurated on 30 August 1859 - it has since become one of the most recognised emblems of Port Louis itself.

title: Central Market Port Louis
about_site_text: The historic heart of Port Louis's daily life, dating to 1839 under British colonial rule (the market itself traces back further, to a 1828 origin before moving to this site in 1833). Its wrought-iron gates, decorated with floral motifs and dating from 1839, are a well-known piece of the city's Victorian-era heritage. The building was heavily renovated between 2001 and 2004 after several fires, while its original character was preserved.
interesting_fact: For nearly two centuries the market has been a meeting point for all of Mauritius's communities - Creole, Franco-Mauritian, Indian, Chinese and African - trading side by side, and it's still often called the Bazaar or Victoria Market by locals.

title: Champ de Mars
about_site_text: Home to the Champ de Mars Racecourse, inaugurated on 25 June 1812 by the Mauritius Turf Club - the oldest horse-racing club in the Southern Hemisphere and the second-oldest in the world. Before it was a racecourse, French governor Mahé de La Bourdonnais used the ground as a military training field for his troops.
interesting_fact: When Mauritius became independent on 12 March 1968, the flag-hoisting ceremony marking the occasion was held here at the Champ de Mars - tying the island's oldest sporting institution to its newest chapter as a nation.

title: Citadelle (Fort Adelaide)
about_site_text: Also known as Fort Adelaide, this hilltop citadel overlooking Port Louis was built by the British between 1830 and 1840, named after Queen Adelaide, consort of King William IV. It was built to guard against invasion and control local unrest amid racial tensions of the period, using hundreds of Indian contractors over six years of construction.
interesting_fact: Despite its imposing basalt-stone walls, the fort was never actually used in combat, and today survives as the best-preserved of the major British fortresses built on the island.

title: Cannon Stand
address: 69 Emmanuel Anquetil St, Port Louis, Mauritius
about_site_text: A row of cast-iron cannons mounted on wooden carriages along the ramparts of the Citadelle (Fort Adelaide), still aimed out over Port Louis harbour just as they were when the fort was completed. Built from black basalt in a Moorish style between 1830 and 1840 under British colonial rule, the fort was raised to guard against a feared French invasion and to help control local opposition to the abolition of slavery, though its guns were, in the end, never fired in anger.
interesting_fact: Despite bristling with cannons and room for a 200-strong garrison, Fort Adelaide never saw combat - it functioned instead as a show of force overlooking the harbour, and today its ramparts are better known as one of the best viewpoints over Port Louis and the surrounding mountains.

title: Blue Penny Museum
about_site_text: A museum dedicated to the history and art of Mauritius, at Caudan Waterfront, opened in November 2001. Its centrepiece is the pair of 1847 "Post Office" stamps - the one-penny orange-red and two-pence blue - among the rarest and most valuable stamps in the world, whose designs were based on Britain's Penny Black and feature Queen Victoria's profile.
interesting_fact: A consortium of Mauritian companies, led by the Mauritius Commercial Bank, paid $2,000,000 in 1993 to buy the stamps back to the island after almost 150 years abroad. To protect them from light damage, the originals are only illuminated for ten minutes on the quarter-past of every opening hour - the rest of the time, visitors see facsimiles.

title: Aapravasi Ghat World Heritage Site
about_site_text: A UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2006, and the place where the modern indentured-labour diaspora began. Built in 1849, the Aapravasi Ghat ("Immigration Depot") was the main entry point for almost 500,000 indentured labourers - mostly from India, but also China, Africa, Madagascar and Southeast Asia - brought to Mauritius between 1849 and 1923, mainly to work the island's sugar plantations after the abolition of slavery.
interesting_fact: Roughly 70% of Mauritians today are descended from these indentured labourers - making this small 1,640 m² depot one of the most significant sites anywhere for understanding the origins of modern Mauritian society, and one of the earliest examples of the labour-migration system that would go on to reshape economies worldwide.

title: Sir Sewoosagur Ramgoolam Statue
about_site_text: A statue at Caudan Waterfront of Sir Seewoosagur Ramgoolam, the first Prime Minister of independent Mauritius. Born in 1900 at Belle Rive to an indentured labourer from India, he rose from a self-enrolled mission-school pupil to co-found the Mauritius Labour Party in 1936, campaigning for voting and workers' rights. He served as Mayor of Port Louis, Chief Minister and Premier before leading Mauritius to independence on 12 March 1968 as its first Prime Minister, later serving as Governor-General - a journey still celebrated as the model of the nation's founding story.
interesting_fact: As the first head of the independent government, Ramgoolam established free education, free healthcare and a national social security system - a legacy still commemorated with wreath-laying ceremonies held at statues like this one, and remembered every year on his birthday, 12 September, celebrated as SSR's birth anniversary.

title: Port Louis Fire Station
about_site_text: The Port Louis Fire and Rescue Service's main station, a working municipal building housed in a handsome colonial-era structure dating to 1906 - the oldest fire station still in operation in Mauritius. It replaced an earlier station relocated from the port area in 1850, part of the city's long, hard-won response to the devastating fires of 1816 and 1892 that tore through Port Louis when most buildings were still made of wood and straw.
interesting_fact: The station's watch tower once served as a lookout for spotting fires across the city before modern communications existed, and it still houses one of only three surviving Merryweather clocks in the world - a rare mechanical relic from the early era of organised firefighting.

title: Café du Vieux Conseil
address: Rue du Vieux Conseil, Port Louis, Mauritius
about_site_text: A colonial-era courtyard café on Rue du Vieux Conseil ("Old Council Street"), tucked among the historic government-quarter buildings near Government House. Housed in an old Port Louis institution with a veranda and timber kiosks shaded by large trees, the courtyard doubles as a venue for lunches, concerts, exhibitions and evening events alongside its regular menu of Mauritian, Indian and Italian dishes.
interesting_fact: The chef's specialty is a pancake served with either asparagus or thinly sliced smoked marlin - a small sign of how thoroughly French, Indian and Mauritian culinary traditions blend together on a single menu here.

title: Port Louis Theatre
address: Remy Ollier St & Jules Koenig St, Port Louis, Mauritius
about_site_text: The Port Louis Theatre, the oldest theatre in the Indian Ocean region. Governor Robert Farquhar laid its first stone in 1820, and architect Pierre Poujade built it in the style of classic London playhouses, with the theatre inaugurated on 11 June 1822. Inside, three tiers of seating for around 600 sit beneath an ornately painted dome ceiling of cherubs and chandeliers, and for over a century it was the island's sole home for opera, drama and balls, until the Plaza Theatre opened in Rose Hill in 1933.
interesting_fact: The idea of bringing theatre to Mauritius dates back even earlier than the building itself - a French warship's health officer first brought a troupe to perform in Port Louis in 1790, though it was disbanded just two years later by a smallpox epidemic.

title: Aurelie Perrine Passenger Terminal
about_site_text: A passenger ferry terminal on the Port Louis waterfront, run by the Mauritius Ports Authority and operated by Mauritius Shipping Corporation under the Coraline service. From here, the ms Mauritius Trochetia sails several times a month to Rodrigues and Reunion Island, carrying both passengers and cargo, making the terminal the main sea link between mainland Mauritius and its outer islands. Facilities include a canteen, money changer and duty-free shop for travellers.
interesting_fact: The crossing to Rodrigues, roughly 560km east across open ocean, takes about 36 hours outbound and around 24 hours on the return leg (longer in rough seas) - a reminder that for most of the year the Mauritius Trochetia is Rodrigues's lifeline for both people and freight, alongside its short air link.

title: Eastern Roche Bois Cemetery
about_site_text: A historic public cemetery at the eastern edge of Port Louis, in the Roche Bois neighbourhood close to the docks, entered through a dark basalt archway topped with a cross. Rows of graves stretch back beneath the palms, reflecting generations of the city's residents, and the site is also recognised by the Commonwealth War Graves Commission for the burials it holds.
interesting_fact: Tucked among the older graves are two Commonwealth war burials from the First World War, their granite headstones maintained by the CWGC - one near the entrance, the other by the boundary wall in the section marked 'E2'.

title: Fort George
about_site_text: The site of Fort George, the largest stone fortification ever built in Mauritius, guarding the northern entrance to Port Louis harbour. A fortification has stood on this ground since Mahe de Labourdonnais's time in 1730, but the British rebuilt it in earnest in the 19th century - named for King George III and IV - both to deter a French attack and to keep the island's slave-owning planters in check after the 1831 Mauritius Rebellion. By 1882 it carried a mix of upgraded Rifled Muzzle Loading guns, making it the most heavily armed post at the harbour mouth.
interesting_fact: Fort George was declared a national monument in 1998 and reconfirmed as national heritage in 2003, but much of the site has fallen into serious disrepair - heritage campaigners have pushed for years to save what remains of Mauritius's largest stone fort from being lost for good.

title: Christian Decotter Cruise Terminal
about_site_text: A cruise-ship passenger terminal on the Port Louis waterfront at Les Salines, named after Christian Decotter, a Mauritian aviation and tourism figure who spent decades in commercial aviation and travel management with companies including Rogers and MTTB, and headed the Concorde travel agency from 1979. Renovated and reopened in 2008, the terminal was the first in the region able to berth the world's largest cruise ships, cementing Port Louis Harbour's role as the premier cruise hub of the Indian Ocean - a 7,500-square-metre facility able to process up to 4,000 passengers at peak times across two access bridges.
interesting_fact: Decotter became the public face of Mauritian tourism policy in the 1990s: spokesperson for the PMSD party, then appointed Chairman of the Tourism Advisory Board in March 1995 under Minister Xavier-Luc Duval. Off duty he was a keen sportsman - a competitive volleyball and basketball player and multiple island tennis-tournament winner - before his death in July 2003.

title: Pere Laval Church & Museum
address: 27 Ste Croix Rd, Port Louis, Mauritius
about_site_text: A major Catholic pilgrimage shrine in the Sainte-Croix district, built around the tomb of Father Jacques-Desire Laval - a French missionary priest and trained doctor who spent nearly 23 years ministering to Mauritius's recently freed slaves and is credited with converting 67,000 people to Christianity. Known as the 'Apostle of Mauritius', he died on 9 September 1864, and more than thirty thousand mourners followed his casket to the tomb opposite the church where it still lies today. He was beatified by Pope John Paul II in 1979, and the site is often described as the Lourdes of the Indian Ocean, with numerous miracles attributed to pilgrims who have visited.
interesting_fact: Every 8 September, people set out from across Mauritius on foot for an overnight march to reach the shrine by his feast day on the 9th - tens of thousands of pilgrims of every faith, some travelling from as far as France, South Africa and Britain, gather to mark the anniversary of his death.

title: Plateau
about_site_text: A scenic elevated vantage point ('Le Plateau') above Port Louis, off Military Road, looking out over the packed rooftops of the capital down to the harbour and Indian Ocean beyond. The name reflects the area's role in the city's history: after repeated disasters in Port Louis itself - the great fire of 1816, recurring malaria outbreaks and cyclones - much of the population moved up to this cooler, healthier central plateau, and many residents still live on these slopes today.
interesting_fact: On a clear day the view stretches from the high-rise towers of the city centre, past the harbour's cranes and cargo ships, all the way out to the open ocean - a single sightline over more than two centuries of Port Louis's growth from a fire-prone colonial port to a modern capital.

title: Viewpoint of Port-Louis
about_site_text: A lookout point atop Signal Mountain (Montagne des Signaux), a 323-metre peak overlooking Port Louis, reached by a tarred road that makes it the easiest of the island's peaks to climb on foot or by vehicle. The mountain takes its name from a French-era signal post once used to relay news of approaching ships to the harbour below, since replaced by a modern antenna farm.
interesting_fact: The signal station here dates to the French colonial period, when lookouts used flag signals from the summit to alert Port Louis merchants to incoming ships hours before they reached the harbour.

title: Rajiv Gandhi Science Center
address: Old Moka Rd, Port Louis, Mauritius
about_site_text: An interactive science museum in Port Louis built through Indian government assistance, aimed at kindling scientific curiosity among young Mauritians through hands-on exhibits, models and outreach programmes. It supplements formal school science education and hosts lectures, seminars and science fairs for the public.
interesting_fact: The centre traces back to a 1994 Trust Fund Act; its foundation stone was laid in 1995 in the presence of Sonia Gandhi, and it finally opened to the public on 30 November 2004, a decade after the enabling legislation was passed.

title: La Tour Koenig
about_site_text: A stone tower built in the early 19th century by Henry Koenig, a founder of the Mauritius Commercial Bank, as a gift for his Bavarian-born father to remind him of the windmills of his homeland - it was never a functioning mill. Standing about 17 metres tall in a Limousin stonework style unique on the island, it is now a national monument managed by the National Heritage Fund, within the grounds of the Nelson Mandela Cultural Centre.
interesting_fact: The tower was left permanently unfinished after a worker fell to his death while placing its fifth carved stone coping - construction was never resumed.

title: Martello Tower
about_site_text: A squat coastal defence tower built by the British between 1832 and 1835, one of five raised around Mauritius after the 1810 conquest from France amid fears of a French counter-attack. Its design copied the Torra di Mortella in Corsica, which had impressed British forces for its thick basalt walls, flat gun roof and self-contained garrison quarters. Restored in 1992 with funding from the Mauritian government and several foreign missions, it reopened as a museum in 2000 and is now a protected national heritage site.
interesting_fact: Despite being purpose-built for war, none of Mauritius's Martello towers ever fired a shot in anger - they were rendered obsolete by advances in artillery before any French attack materialised.

title: Memoire Des Naufrages Du Stargate
about_site_text: A memorial to the ten people who died when the pleasure boat Stargate sank in rough seas near Baie-du-Tombeau while returning from a day trip to Île Plate, off the north coast. Fourteen young holidaymakers and crew were aboard; only four survived. The tragedy led to manslaughter charges against the boat's owner, Donald Veerabadren, over the vessel's seaworthiness.
interesting_fact: Among the ten who died was the boat's own skipper, Mamode Dowlut, alongside nine young passengers including Irsand Pokun, Israq Khodabux and Yashill Oozeer - names still listed on the memorial.

title: Les Salines Garden
about_site_text: A public garden in the Les Salines district, named for a saltworks founded on the site in 1726 by salt-worker Jean Dominique Michel de Caudan during the era of Governor Mahé de Labourdonnais - salt was a vital commodity then, used to preserve meat for ships' stores. Also known as Robert Edward Hart Garden, it later became a pleasure ground and place of relaxation for Port Louis residents, and the district still holds Kwan Tee Pagoda, the oldest Chinese temple on the island, founded in 1842.
interesting_fact: The salt pans that gave the district its name were founded in 1726, more than a decade before Port Louis itself became the island's capital under Labourdonnais in the 1730s.

title: Tortoise Park
about_site_text: A small tortoise enclosure in Port Louis, most likely home to Aldabra giant tortoises - a conservation-minded attraction of a type found at several sites around Mauritius. Fittingly, Port Louis itself was dubbed the 'Harbour of Tortoises' by early Dutch sailors who anchored here from 1606, giving any tortoise display in the capital a nice historical echo, even if this particular park's own founding history is not independently documented.

title: Lenin Statue Bust
about_site_text: A bronze bust of Vladimir Lenin standing in a small square in Port Louis, an unlikely sight for a tropical island tour. It commemorates the Soviet Union's early recognition of Mauritian independence and Cold War-era ties between the two countries - one of the more unexpected monuments a visitor can stumble across in the capital.
interesting_fact: The bust was installed in 1983 in what is known locally as Yuri Gagarin Square, named after the Soviet cosmonaut - making it a small cluster of Soviet-linked commemoration in one corner of Port Louis.

title: Cimetiere de l'Ouest
about_site_text: The Western Cemetery of Port Louis, established in 1771 after its predecessor near the Pouce stream was closed over fears of infection - it was originally known as the Cimetière du Fort Blanc, after a nearby fort. Its ornate Creole, French and British tombstones and mausoleums chart the island's colonial history, though the cemetery, expanded to 60,000 square metres, was still overwhelmed by the catastrophic 1865-67 malaria epidemic that killed roughly a third of Port Louis's population.
interesting_fact: The cemetery started out covering just 600 square metres in 1771 - a hundredth the size it eventually grew to as the city's burial needs multiplied over the following century.

title: 1892 Hurricane Memorial
about_site_text: A memorial to the catastrophic cyclone of 29 April 1892, which struck Mauritius with winds over 195 km/h and remains one of the deadliest tropical cyclones ever recorded in the Southern Hemisphere. Roughly a third of Port Louis was flattened, some 1,500 houses were wrecked, 20,000 residents left homeless, and at least 596 people died in the city alone - out of about 1,200 deaths across the island.
interesting_fact: The storm was powerful enough to snap the stone tomb-monument of Governor Malartic in Champ de Mars clean in two, a small but telling sign of just how violently the 1892 cyclone tore through the capital.

title: Marina
about_site_text: A working small-boat marina on the Port Louis waterfront - locally known as "Bassin des Chaloupes" (basin of the whaleboats) - built as part of the Caudan Waterfront development that opened in 1996. It offers around 20 berths with power, water, showers and laundry facilities, with depths shifting between roughly 2 and 4 metres at low tide, and sits below the backdrop of the Moka mountain range, with fishing boats and pleasure craft moored side by side.
interesting_fact: Port Louis is Mauritius's only official port of entry for yachts arriving from across the Indian Ocean - every visiting vessel must first clear Health, Immigration and Customs at the Customs Landing Steps in the main harbour (a fixed sequence that can take under an hour with an agent) before it's allowed to move here to the marina itself, and the commercial port only opens to arriving traffic between 6am and 6pm.

title: Le Suffren Hotel & Marina
about_site_text: A 4-star hotel on the Caudan Waterfront with its own marina, named after Pierre André de Suffren, the 18th-century French admiral who used Île de France (as Mauritius was then called) as his forward base while fighting the British for control of the Indian Ocean during the 1780s. Its nautical-themed rooms and harbour-facing terraces trade on that seafaring history at the water's edge of Port Louis.
interesting_fact: Suffren arrived at Île de France in July 1781 to resupply his squadron before waging an inconclusive but fiercely fought naval campaign against Britain's Vice-Admiral Edward Hughes - the same rivalry the hotel's name still nods to over two centuries later.

title: Meat Market
about_site_text: The butchery section of Port Louis's Central Market, on this site since the market moved to La Corderie Street in 1833, within a building whose gates and cast-iron colonial architecture were inaugurated by Governor Sir William Gomm in 1844. Physically separated from the market's adjoining fish and fresh-produce halls, it supplies much of the capital's daily cooking, and its trade largely follows halal practice, reflecting the sizeable Muslim community concentrated in this part of Port Louis. Trading starts well before dawn, with the busiest activity long over by the time most of the city's shops open for the day.
interesting_fact: The oldest surviving building of Central Market dates to 1833 - meaning shoppers here are buying meat in a structure that predates the abolition of slavery in Mauritius (effective 1 February 1835, when 66,343 people were freed) by about two years.

title: Fish Market
about_site_text: The fish and seafood section of Central Market Port Louis, opening from around 6am each day as fishermen bring in their catch from the Indian Ocean - octopus (fresh and dried), shark, wahoo, marlin, lobster and more. Unlike the fixed-price stalls elsewhere in the market, this section still runs on an auction system, with fishmongers calling out and haggling over the price of each morning's catch in full view of shoppers - a louder, livelier way of trading than anywhere else in the market complex.
interesting_fact: The market's fish auctions happen daily at dawn, which means the liveliest trading here is often over before most tourists - and even most Port Louis office workers - have started their day.

title: Rabita Hall
address: 28 Pope Hennessy St, Port Louis, Mauritius
about_site_text: An event and function hall in central Port Louis, on Pope Hennessy Street close to St James Cathedral, the Supreme Court and the passport office, run by the Muslim Educational Society - a community organisation founded in 1926 by Mawlana Abdullah Rashid Nawab. Alongside weddings, community gatherings and religious lectures, the hall anchors a wider network of educational and social programmes the Society runs across the capital.
interesting_fact: The same Society behind Rabita Hall also runs the Rabita Prevocational School, set up in 1999 to give young girls who have dropped out of mainstream education practical skills training and a path back into work - a reminder that a hall best known for weddings is also the public face of a century-old charitable network.

title: Tombeau Malartic
about_site_text: An obelisk-tomb in the grounds of Champ de Mars racecourse, raised in 1800 by the colonial administration for Anne Joseph Hippolyte de Maurès, Comte de Malartic, who governed the French territories east of the Cape of Good Hope from 1792 until his death in Port Louis on 28 July 1800. He was popular enough in office that the city's main street was later renamed Rue Malartic in his honour.
interesting_fact: The 1892 cyclone was violent enough to snap Malartic's stone tomb-monument clean in two - a small but telling measure of just how destructive that storm was in Champ de Mars.

title: Port Louis Gymkhana
address: Frère Felix De Valois St, Port Louis, Mauritius
about_site_text: A social and sporting club in the British colonial 'gymkhana club' tradition, part of a model the Empire exported across its colonies from Africa to the Caribbean and Asia. Mauritius's gymkhana golf course, one of the oldest in the Southern Hemisphere, has hosted golf since 1844, when it began life as a service club for officers of the British Royal Navy stationed on the island.
interesting_fact: The club's golf course has been played continuously since 1844, making it roughly contemporary with Port Louis's Central Market and one of the oldest sporting grounds anywhere in the Indian Ocean region.

title: Tien Tan Chinese Pagoda
address: Foot of Signal Mountain, near Chinatown, Port Louis, Mauritius
about_site_text: A Chinese Buddhist and Taoist temple at the foot of Signal Mountain, on the edge of Port Louis's Chinatown district, built in the 1960s as a scaled-down replica of Beijing's famous Temple of Heaven (Tian Tan), from which it takes its name - also written locally as Thien-Thane Pagode. A bright red staircase leads up to the temple against the green backdrop of the mountain, and inside there are no statues, only an altar where the faithful leave offerings beneath softly glowing lanterns and intricately carved decoration.
interesting_fact: Unlike most pagodas, which are filled with statues of deities, the inside of Tien Tan Pagoda is deliberately bare but for a single altar - visitors come to light incense and leave offerings rather than to view religious imagery, in keeping with its Taoist roots.

title: La Butte Glissement de terrain
about_site_text: A site marking La Butte, one of Port Louis's recognised landslide-risk zones, where steep basalt slopes and clay-rich soils have repeatedly given way after heavy rain or nearby construction work. The area has been monitored and studied by the municipality and engineering researchers for years as part of wider efforts to manage landslide hazards across the city.
interesting_fact: In August 2017, excavation work for the Metro Express rail project triggered a landslide at La Butte that cracked a road, brought down a utility pylon and damaged nearby walls - a vivid, recent example of why the site is flagged as high-risk.

title: Street Art and Murals
address: 26 Dr Sun Yat Sen St, Port Louis, Mauritius
about_site_text: A cluster of colourful murals along Dr Sun Yat Sen Street and the adjoining alley nicknamed 'Manga Street' (Venpin Street), in Port Louis's Chinatown. The artwork - including a giant dragon, a Bruce Lee portrait and anime-style characters - grew out of a revitalisation drive begun in 2005 by the New Chinatown Foundation, a group of young residents determined to breathe new life into a once run-down district.
interesting_fact: Many of the murals here were painted to mark the 50th anniversary of bilateral ties between Mauritius and China, turning a once-neglected back alley into one of the most photographed spots in Port Louis.

title: Square Khadafi
address: 51 Madad ul Islam St, Port Louis, Mauritius
about_site_text: A public square in Plaine Verte, Port Louis's Muslim quarter, popularly known as Khadafi Square after Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi donated a statue of himself to the city here in the 1980s, reflecting Libyan-Mauritian ties of that era. The statue was removed after Gaddafi's fall from power in 2011, but the square has kept his name and remains a community gathering point for the neighbourhood.
interesting_fact: The statue that gave the square its name outlasted Gaddafi's own rule by only months - it came down soon after his 2011 overthrow and death, yet locals still call the square by his name today.

title: Old Ghoon Mazaar
about_site_text: A mazaar (shrine to a revered holy figure) on Benares Street in Plaine Verte, the historic Muslim quarter of Port Louis that sits on the far side of the Citadelle hill. The district is the traditional home of the Ghoon (or Yamsé) festival, observed since 1790 by Mauritius's Shia Muslim minority to commemorate the martyrdom of Hussain, grandson of the Prophet Muhammad, during the Islamic month of Muharram.
interesting_fact: The Ghoon festival tradition in Plaine Verte dates back to 1790 - old enough that Mauritius was still Île de France under French rule when it began, and it has been observed here through French, British and independent Mauritian eras alike.

title: Islamic Cultural Centre
about_site_text: A community centre serving Port Louis's Muslim community, established in August 1987 to meet a long-felt need for a dedicated cultural institution, in line with the Mauritian government's policy of promoting the cultural heritage of all communities on the island. It was placed on a formal legal footing two years later through the Islamic Cultural Centre Trust Fund Act, proclaimed on 15 December 1989 and subsequently amended several times.
interesting_fact: The Centre's founding legislation has been amended three times since 1989 - in 1991, 2000 and 2001 - reflecting how its role expanded over more than three decades.

title: FORENA (Fondation Ressources et Nature) - Endemic tree plantation
about_site_text: A reforestation site near the Citadelle (Fort Adelaide), planted with endemic Mauritian species by FORENA, a local environmental NGO working to restore the island's native forest cover. The hill has suffered serious soil erosion linked to climate change, and FORENA's plan covers roughly 11-12 hectares of the Citadelle's slopes as part of a wider mission that has planted over 20,000 endemic trees and replanted more than 20 hectares across Mauritius.
interesting_fact: FORENA's broader restoration work has earned it over 20 Bio ECOcert organic-farming certifications alongside its tree-planting - a sign the foundation pairs reforestation with sustainable agriculture training for local communities.

title: Statue de Saint Louis
address: St. Louis Cathedral's Garden, Pope Hennessy St, Port Louis, Mauritius
about_site_text: A statue of Saint Louis (King Louis IX of France) standing in the garden of St Louis Cathedral, honouring the city and cathedral's namesake saint. It provides a quiet, reflective spot in the cathedral grounds, framed by the church's striking facade and well-kept gardens in the heart of Port Louis.

title: Photographic Museum Of Mauritius
address: Rue du Vieux Conseil, Port Louis, Mauritius
about_site_text: A museum of historic photography on Rue du Vieux Conseil, founded in 1966 by photographer Tristan Bréville and his wife to preserve the island's photographic memory since 1839. Housed in an 18th-century building that once belonged to French botanist and administrator Pierre Poivre, it holds over 50,000 old photographs of Mauritius along with a collection of historic cameras and equipment.
interesting_fact: Among its collection is one of the rarest lenses in photographic history, made by Charles Chevalier for Jacques Daguerre - inventor of the daguerreotype - in 1834, just a few years before photography itself was publicly unveiled.

title: National Assembly of the Republic of Mauritius
address: National Assembly, Intendance St, Port Louis, Mauritius
about_site_text: The seat of the Mauritian parliament on Intendance Street, housed in the historic New Treasury Building next to Government House - itself the oldest building in the capital, dating to 1738 when Governor Mahé de Labourdonnais rebuilt it in stone. The Legislative Council has met on this site since 1875, a lineage that runs directly through to today's democratically elected National Assembly.
interesting_fact: Lawmakers have been meeting on this exact site since 1875 - nearly 150 years of continuous legislative history, spanning French colonial rule, the British Empire and an independent Mauritius.

title: Natural History Museum
about_site_text: The Mauritius Institute's Natural History Museum, on the ground floor of a National Heritage building constructed between 1880 and 1884 and modelled partly on Sri Lanka's Colombo Museum. Its collections trace back to 1826, when naturalists Julien Desjardins and Louis Bouton first proposed a museum to the governor - the resulting Desjardins Museum opened in 1842, decades before the current building existed, and the institution was declared a National Museum in 2000.
interesting_fact: The museum's most complete dodo skeleton was not unearthed until 1904, discovered by a Port Louis barber named Étienne Thirioux, whose amateur fossil-hunting turned up one of the best specimens of the extinct bird ever found.

title: Église Adventiste Du Septième Jour Port-Louis
address: St Louis St, Port Louis, Mauritius
about_site_text: A Seventh-day Adventist congregation on St Louis Street, part of a Protestant denomination formally organised in 1863 out of mid-19th-century Christian eschatological movements. Distinctively, Adventists worship on Saturdays rather than Sundays and are active locally in health, education and humanitarian work, alongside the denomination's emphasis on Biblical authority.

title: La Galerie du Génie
address: 6 Edith Cavell St, Port Louis, Mauritius
about_site_text: A 602-square-metre exhibition and events space on Edith Cavell Street, inside an 18th-century building originally known as the Hôtel du Génie. It now hosts art exhibitions, markets and concerts as part of EDITH, a cultural venue aiming to make the space Port Louis's community meeting point for the local arts scene.
interesting_fact: The building once served as storage for the survey maps of Jean Baptiste Lislet Geoffroy, the island's pioneering 18th-century hydrographic engineer - making a space now devoted to contemporary art the former archive of some of Mauritius's earliest scientific cartography.

title: The Bank of Mauritius Museum
address: Sir William Newton St, Port Louis, Mauritius
about_site_text: A museum on the history of currency in Mauritius, run by the country's central bank inside its original premises on Sir William Newton Street. It opened on 3 March 2018, marking the 50th anniversary of both the Bank of Mauritius and Mauritian independence, and displays around 500 artefacts spanning from the 12th-century Arab period through to the present, drawn together with contributions from the MCB Group, HSBC Mauritius, the Royal Mint and banknote maker Thomas De La Rue.
interesting_fact: Among the museum's prized pieces is the Piastre Decaen - the only coin ever minted in Mauritius itself, and the only coin ever struck by France outside mainland France for use in one of its colonies.

title: Queen Victoria Statue
about_site_text: A statue of Queen Victoria standing at Place d'Armes in front of Government House, erected in 1897 during the height of the British colonial era on the island. Its inscription reads 'To the memory of beloved and much regretted Queen Victoria Empress of India - the Inhabitants of Mauritius', reflecting the formal affection colonial-era Mauritius expressed toward the monarch.
interesting_fact: The statue was raised in 1897, the same year Victoria marked her Diamond Jubilee - 60 years on the throne - meaning Mauritius's tribute went up as similar Victoria statues were being unveiled across the British Empire to mark the same milestone.

title: Statue of William Newton
about_site_text: A statue of Sir William Newton (1842-1915), a Mauritian lawyer of mixed Indo-Mauritian and Scottish descent who led the reformist movement launched in 1882 demanding an elected element in the colonial Legislative Council. His campaigning under the administration of Governor Sir John Pope Hennessy helped bring about the Constitutional Reform of 1885, which for the first time let Indo-Mauritians and other non-white islanders elect their own representatives.
interesting_fact: The Constitution Newton helped win came into force on 20 October 1885 - the first time in Mauritian history that non-white islanders could vote for their own representatives in the colonial legislature.

title: Statue of Sir John Pope Hennessy
about_site_text: A statue of Sir John Pope Hennessy, an Irish-born colonial administrator who served as Governor of Mauritius from 1883 to 1889. Regarded as a progressive and liberal governor by the standards of his time, his administration presided over the reformist movement that produced the 1885 Constitutional Reform, extending the vote to Indo-Mauritian and other non-white islanders for the first time.
interesting_fact: Before Mauritius, Pope Hennessy had already governed the Bahamas, Barbados and Hong Kong - Mauritius was one stop in an unusually well-travelled career administering four very different corners of the British Empire.

title: China Town Gate
about_site_text: One of the ornamental Friendship Gates marking the entrance to Port Louis's Chinatown on Royal Road, one of the oldest Chinatowns in Africa. The gates were a gift from Foshan, in Guangdong province, Port Louis's twin city in China, symbolising the long-standing links between the two places and the wider friendship between Mauritius and China.
interesting_fact: Chinatown's roots reach back to the 1780s, when the first Chinese migrants arrived in Port Louis from Guangzhou aboard British, French and Danish ships - making it one of the oldest continuously inhabited Chinese communities anywhere in Africa.

title: Intercontinental Slavery Museum
about_site_text: A museum documenting the history of slavery and indentured labour in the Indian Ocean, opened on 4 September 2023 inside Port Louis's former military hospital - the oldest building in the city, constructed between 1736 and 1740 under Governor Mahé de Labourdonnais, reportedly by enslaved labour. Its exhibits include objects unearthed from the old slave cemetery at Albion during 2021-22 excavations, alongside 63 ethnographic plaster busts cast in 1846 from the faces of enslaved people from Mauritius, Tanzania and the Comoros.
interesting_fact: The museum's 63 plaster busts, made in 1846 by Eugène de Froberville, were cast directly from the faces of enslaved individuals - an unusually direct and unsettling physical record of people who left almost no other trace in the historical archive.

title: Mauritius Postal Museum
address: Port Louis Waterfront, Trunk Road, Port Louis, Mauritius
about_site_text: A museum tracing the island's postal history, in a mid-Victorian building on the waterfront built between 1865 and 1870 and listed as a national monument since 1958. It served as Mauritius's main post office from December 1870 (and gained the Central Telegraph Office in 1877) before being converted into a museum in 2008, covering postal services from the Dutch and French periods through British rule.
interesting_fact: In 1846, Mauritius became the fifth country in the world - and the first British colony - to require prepayment of postage using stamps, producing the famous Penny Red and Two Pence Blue, the same stamps now celebrated at the nearby Blue Penny Museum.

title: Alte Windmühle (Windmill Museum)
about_site_text: Port Louis's historic waterfront windmill, built in 1736 to grind flour for dockworkers in the harbour - a French-style mill with four sails and a pointed cap. After the British took the island in 1810 it was repurposed as a signal tower, then abandoned for much of the 20th century before being restored to full working order in 1998 with help from the French windmill association ARAM. It has operated as a small museum around the restored mill since 1999.
interesting_fact: The mill sat derelict for most of the 20th century before French millwrights' association ARAM helped bring it back to full working condition in 1998 - meaning it can technically still grind flour today, over 280 years after it was built.

title: SBM Fountain
about_site_text: A dancing fountain on the Port Louis waterfront, donated by the State Bank of Mauritius as part of a revamp of the waterfront masterminded by developer Landscope Mauritius. Lit and choreographed to music in the evenings, it was conceived as a symbol of unity and harmony among Mauritius's diverse communities.

title: SAJ Statue
about_site_text: A bronze statue of Sir Anerood Jugnauth ('SAJ'), unveiled at the Port Louis Waterfront on 15 June 2024, honouring the former Prime Minister and President who dominated Mauritian politics for decades. It stands beside an earlier statue of Sir Seewoosagur Ramgoolam, placing two of independent Mauritius's most prominent leaders side by side on the same esplanade.
interesting_fact: At 3.6 metres tall, the SAJ statue was built about 30 centimetres taller than the neighbouring Ramgoolam statue, and its Rs 13.5 million cost and sculptor Devanand Bungshee's likeness both drew public criticism at the time of unveiling.

title: Bust of Queen Victoria
about_site_text: A bust of Queen Victoria near the Port Louis waterfront, distinct from the full-length Queen Victoria Statue that stands at Place d'Armes in front of Government House (erected 1897). Like that statue, it dates from an era when such colonial-era tributes to the monarch were common across British territories.

title: Victoria Metro Station
address: Place Victoria Bus Terminal, Port Louis, Mauritius
about_site_text: The starting terminus of the Metro Express, Mauritius's modern light-rail network, at the Place Victoria transport hub in central Port Louis. Phase 1, running from Port Louis Victoria to Rose Hill Central, opened on 3 October 2019 with full commercial service from 10 January 2020, and the station now connects seamlessly to buses, taxis and a pedestrian bridge to Caudan Waterfront.
interesting_fact: Port Louis actually had a railway well over a century before the Metro Express - the island's first line opened in 1864, running some 50 km north and east from Port Louis via Roche Bois, Pamplemousses and Flacq.

title: Caudan Arts Centre
about_site_text: A performing-arts venue at Caudan Waterfront built on what was once a car park, inaugurated in December 2018 as the first new theatre built in Mauritius in nearly a century. Its 431-seat auditorium, designed by architect Maurice Giraud and Didier Ho Architecture with acoustics engineering by Arup, hosts drama, music and dance, alongside a restaurant, bars, a conference room and exhibition space.
interesting_fact: Before this venue opened in 2018, Mauritius had gone almost 100 years without a purpose-built theatre - making the Caudan Arts Centre the first new stage of its kind on the island in nearly a century.

title: MCine Port-Louis Waterfront
about_site_text: A multiplex cinema at Caudan Waterfront with three screens seating around 550 people, screening a mix of Hollywood and Bollywood releases with 7.1 Dolby Digital sound. It shares the harbour-front entertainment strip with a second cinema, Star Caudan, making Caudan Waterfront the main hub for film-going in Port Louis.

title: Port Louis Casino
about_site_text: A casino at Caudan Waterfront, part of the complex that opened on 25 November 1996 on land once occupied by warehouses and a meteorological observatory. It occupies the Barkly Wharf building, named for Sir Henry Barkly, Governor of Mauritius from 1863 to 1870, and is known for a striking facade styled like the bow of a pirate ship, complete with bowsprit mast and statuary.
interesting_fact: The casino building's pirate-ship facade - a bowsprit mast and figurehead-style statues built into the architecture - makes it one of the more theatrical pieces of commercial design anywhere on the Port Louis waterfront.

title: Craft Market
about_site_text: The craft market at Caudan Waterfront, selling Mauritian handicrafts, textiles and souvenirs within the wider complex that opened on 25 November 1996. The Caudan development itself takes its name from Jean Dominique Michel de Caudan, who arrived from Languedoc and established a saltpan near this stretch of coast back in 1726.
interesting_fact: The Caudan area's recorded history as commercial ground stretches back to 1726, when its namesake founded a saltworks here - two and a half centuries before the site became a modern shopping and crafts destination.

title: Umbrella Square
about_site_text: A pedestrian stretch at Caudan Waterfront transformed into a photogenic "umbrella sky" by a canopy of colourful open umbrellas suspended overhead, creating a floating rainbow ceiling and dappled shade below. Also known as Umbrella Street, the installation follows a globally popular format - the Umbrella Sky Project - that began in the Portuguese town of Agueda in 2011 and has since spread to public spaces on several continents. It has become one of the most-photographed spots on the Port Louis waterfront, its playful modern art sitting against the backdrop of the city's older port heritage.
interesting_fact: The original Umbrella Sky Project in Agueda, Portugal, was inspired by the 1964 film Mary Poppins - Port Louis's version adapts that very European idea to a tropical setting, where the umbrellas do double duty shading pedestrians from the sun as much as decorating the walkway.

title: Place du Caudan and Caudan Waterfront
about_site_text: Place du Caudan is a small plaza within the wider Caudan Waterfront development, which opened on 25 November 1996 on former docklands and has since become one of Port Louis's most popular spots for both tourists and locals - a lively mix of restaurants, bars and a shopping mall along the harbour, dotted with statues, fountains and public art, including a statue of Sir Seewoosagur Ramgoolam, independent Mauritius's first Prime Minister. The whole waterfront takes its name from Jean Dominique Michel de Caudan, a saltpan worker ("saunier") from Languedoc in France who set up a saltpan here in 1726, on what was then a small coral islet and bay southwest of the young settlement - over the next two and a half centuries the site went on to host a gunpowder magazine, an astronomical and meteorological observatory, warehouses and dry docks, long before any of today's restaurants and shops arrived.
interesting_fact: The saltpan that gave Caudan its name has left its own trace nearby - it's remembered today in the Robert Edward Hart Garden, on the road leading into the waterfront, close to where Jean de Caudan once evaporated seawater for salt almost two centuries before the first shopping mall was ever built on this stretch of harbour.

title: Swing Bridge
about_site_text: A bridge over a channel of Port Louis harbour, allowing boat traffic to pass through - part of a working port whose basin was expanded and dredged repeatedly from the late 18th century onward, notably under naval engineer Chevalier de Tromelin in the 1780s and under Governor Decaen's improvements in the early 1800s. The port's infrastructure kept growing through the 19th century, with the Mauritius Dock added in 1857, the Stevenson Dry Dock in 1859 and the Albion Dock in 1860, as Port Louis became one of the busiest reprovisioning stops on the sailing route between Europe and Asia.

title: Odysseo- oceanarium (Mauritius) LTD
about_site_text: Mauritius's first and largest oceanarium, a 5,500-square-metre complex on the Port Louis harbour waterfront that opened in 2021. Spread across six themed zones from mangroves to open ocean, its 45 aquariums hold more than 200 marine species, with underwater tunnels, interactive shows, a shark touch-pool and a children's laboratory built around a conservation-education mission.
interesting_fact: Odysseo is the largest oceanarium anywhere in the Mascarene Islands - a distinction that puts this stretch of Port Louis harbour ahead of similar attractions in Réunion and the Seychelles.

title: Statue of Maurice Curé
about_site_text: A statue of Dr Maurice Curé (1886-1977), the medical doctor who conceived and launched the Mauritius Labour Party on 23 February 1936, the island's first mass political party campaigning for the rights of labourers and artisans. He led it for its first five years, until 1941, working alongside co-founders including Emmanuel Anquetil, Barthélemy Ohsan and Pandit Sahadeo before stepping back from leadership.
interesting_fact: Curé trained as a doctor, not a politician - he only turned to founding the Labour Party after returning to Mauritius in 1913 and serving as Municipality of Port Louis's own medical doctor.

title: H.M Borstal
about_site_text: A former juvenile detention facility on the outskirts of Port Louis, whose building was originally constructed by the French as a hospital before being repurposed under British colonial administration as 'Her Majesty's Borstal' - a youth reform institution, part of a system used across the UK and Commonwealth to house and rehabilitate young offenders rather than send them to adult prisons.

title: Musée La Bonté Innée
address: Couvent des Sœurs BPS, Edith Cavell St, Port Louis, Mauritius
about_site_text: A small museum inside the Couvent des Sœurs BPS on Rue Edith Cavell, opened in 2024 to tell the life story of Mère Augustine (born Caroline Lenferna de Laresle, 1824-1900), the Mauritian nun who founded the Congrégation des Sœurs de Charité de Notre-Dame-du-Bon-et-Secours on this same site in 1850. Objects, paintings, photographs and archival documents trace her work and the congregation's long history of healthcare and education on the island.
interesting_fact: During Port Louis's 1854 cholera epidemic, Mère Augustine and two fellow sisters nursed the sick through the outbreak, and that same year she founded the colony's first orphanage, taking in children without distinction of race or colour - a founding act the museum is built around.

title: Jardins de la Compagnie (Company Garden)
about_site_text: Port Louis's oldest and largest public garden, laid out in the 18th century on land first used as a vegetable plot by the French East India Company. Under threat of a smallpox epidemic the ground was pressed into service as a cemetery until the burial ground was moved to the West Cemetery in 1771, after which the site was replanted as an ornamental park. Today its avenues of towering banyan and royal palm trees, fountains and quiet benches make it a favourite lunchtime retreat for office workers in the surrounding capital, and it doubles as an open-air gallery of Mauritian history, dotted with more than a dozen statues and busts of the writers, doctors and independence-era figures who shaped the island.
interesting_fact: Look closely among the trees and you'll find a cluster of individual monuments worth tracking down in their own right, including tributes to journalist Remy Ollier, poet Leoville L'Homme, physiologist Brown-Sequard and civil-rights lawyer Manilal Doctor - each with its own story told elsewhere on this tour.

title: Statue of Remy Ollier
address: Jardins de la Compagnie, Port Louis, Mauritius
about_site_text: A monument in the Company Garden to Remy Ollier (1816-1845), a mixed-race Mauritian journalist often called the father of the island's free press. Barred by his ancestry from full civil rights under colonial rule, Ollier founded the newspaper La Sentinelle de Maurice in 1843 specifically to campaign against the discriminatory laws that denied "free coloured" Mauritians equal status with white colonists, and his agitation helped force reforms within just a few years of the paper's launch.
interesting_fact: Ollier died of tuberculosis in 1845 aged only 28, having spent barely two years as a public campaigner - this monument, unveiled for the centenary of his birth on 15 October 1916, was raised because that brief career was seen as having changed the course of Mauritian civil rights.

title: Statue of Leoville L'Homme
address: Jardins de la Compagnie, Port Louis, Mauritius
about_site_text: A monument to Ephrem Leoville L'Homme (1857-1928), regarded as one of Mauritius's foremost poets and a key figure in the island's 19th-century literary revival. Writing in French at a time when Mauritian literature was rarely taken seriously beyond the island, his poetry gave voice to everyday Mauritian life and helped establish a distinctly local literary identity separate from mainland France.
interesting_fact: The monument stands not far from fellow writer Remy Ollier's in the Company Garden, so the two are easy to visit together - a poet and a pioneering journalist, born a generation apart, now sharing the same quiet stretch of parkland.

title: Statue of Manilal Doctor
address: Jardins de la Compagnie, Port Louis, Mauritius
about_site_text: A life-size statue of Manilal Maganlal Doctor (1881-1956), the Indian barrister sent to Mauritius in 1907 by Mahatma Gandhi himself to provide free legal aid to indentured Indian labourers. Practising at the Supreme Court, Doctor took on bonded workers' cases pro bono and founded the newspaper The Hindustani to campaign for their rights, under the motto "Liberty of Individuals! Fraternity of Men!!! Equality of Race!!!"
interesting_fact: The statue's inscription reads simply "He felt for the oppressed and served them" - it was unveiled in 1959, three years after his death, and is still garlanded by visitors during commemorations, a rare honour among Port Louis's colonial-era monuments.

title: Bust of Charles-Edouard Brown-Sequard
address: Jardins de la Compagnie, Port Louis, Mauritius
about_site_text: A bronze bust honouring Charles-Edouard Brown-Sequard (1817-1894), the Port Louis-born physiologist and neurologist who became one of the 19th century's most influential medical scientists, teaching at the College de France in Paris and first describing the spinal-cord injury pattern now known as Brown-Sequard syndrome.
interesting_fact: Brown-Sequard first studied that syndrome after observing spinal injuries among Mauritian sugarcane cutters back on his home island - this bust in the Company Garden is said to be the only public statue of him anywhere in the world, despite his international scientific reputation.

title: Statue of Adrien d'Epinay
address: Jardins de la Compagnie, Port Louis, Mauritius
about_site_text: A monument in the Company Garden marking the centenary of the death of Adrien d'Epinay (1789-1839), a Mauritian lawyer and politician who led early campaigns against extending civil rights to free people of colour while separately championing planter interests through the compensation negotiations that followed the abolition of slavery - making him one of the most consequential, if controversial, figures in the island's 19th-century political history.
interesting_fact: The monument was raised in 1939, exactly a century after his death, by admirers who saw him as a founder of organised Mauritian politics - a reminder that Port Louis's statues don't only honour reformers, but also the establishment figures reformers like Remy Ollier, whose statue stands nearby, were fighting against.

title: Statue of Ti Frere (Alphonse Ravaton)
address: Jardins de la Compagnie, Port Louis, Mauritius
about_site_text: A statue of Alphonse Ravaton (1900-1992), known to every Mauritian as "Ti Frere" ("Little Brother"), the singer and songwriter widely credited as the father of modern sega - the Creole music and dance style descended from the songs of enslaved and indentured labourers that later became Mauritius's national music.
interesting_fact: Ti Frere spent much of his life working as a labourer and only found wide fame late in life, in the 1960s and 70s, when folklorists began recording him - this statue, unveiled 28 April 2000, celebrates a musician who was, for decades, more famous among ordinary Mauritians than any politician.

title: Bust of Raoul Rivet
address: Jardins de la Compagnie, Port Louis, Mauritius
about_site_text: A bust of Raoul Rivet, a Franco-Mauritian journalist and writer, inscribed with his own words "Je dois a la France d'etre un homme pensant" ("I owe to France the fact that I am a thinking man") - a tribute to the French cultural and literary education that shaped Mauritius's colonial-era intelligentsia.
interesting_fact: The bust was unveiled on 18 September 1980, more than a decade after Mauritian independence in 1968, showing how the island's French cultural heritage continued to be publicly honoured even after the colonial relationship with France itself had ended two centuries earlier.

title: Monument to Soeur Marie Barthelemy
address: Jardins de la Compagnie, Port Louis, Mauritius
about_site_text: A monument to Soeur Marie Barthelemy, a Catholic nun remembered in Mauritius as the "mother of the poor" for her charitable work among Port Louis's destitute during the 19th century, in an era when organised social welfare barely existed on the island.
interesting_fact: She died at sea on 17 August 1897, and the road running along this side of the Company Garden - Mere Barthelemy Street - is named after her, meaning her memory is woven into the neighbourhood's street plan as well as this one monument.

title: Al-Idrissi Monument
address: Jardins de la Compagnie, Port Louis, Mauritius
about_site_text: A monument honouring Muhammad al-Idrisi (c.1100-1165), the medieval Arab geographer and cartographer whose 12th-century world map and geographical writings, produced for the Norman court of Sicily, were centuries ahead of their time and remained a key reference for European mapmakers for generations. Its presence in the Company Garden recognises the broader Arab and Islamic contribution to the science of navigation and exploration.
interesting_fact: Unveiled on 8 August 2010, it's one of the newest monuments in the garden and one of very few anywhere in the world honouring al-Idrisi specifically for his cartographic legacy, rather than any direct connection to Mauritius itself.

title: Slavery Abolition Monument
address: Jardins de la Compagnie, Port Louis, Mauritius
about_site_text: A memorial in the Company Garden marking the abolition of slavery in Mauritius, which took effect on 1 February 1835 - more than 20 years after the island passed to British control, and only after the British government paid compensation not to the roughly 70,000 enslaved people freed, but to their former owners.
interesting_fact: Mauritius still marks 1 February every year as Abolition of Slavery Day, a public holiday - making this quiet garden monument a focal point for a commemoration most visitors to the island never see, even though it sits in one of Port Louis's most-visited parks.

title: King Edward VII Statue
address: Champ de Mars Racecourse, Port Louis, Mauritius
about_site_text: A statue of King Edward VII standing within the grounds of the Champ de Mars Racecourse, sculpted by Prosper d'Epinay - the same Mauritian-born sculptor responsible for several of the other historic statues around Port Louis - and erected during the height of British colonial rule to honour the reigning monarch.
interesting_fact: It shares the racecourse grounds with a separate obelisk raised to a French governor, meaning the Champ de Mars quietly commemorates rulers from both the French and British colonial eras inside what is still an active, working racecourse rather than a museum.

title: Kwan Tee Pagoda
about_site_text: Built by the Chinese community in 1842 in what is now Port Louis's Chinatown district, Kwan Tee Pagoda is honoured as the oldest pagoda in the Southern Hemisphere and on the African continent. It's dedicated to Kwan Tee (Guan Di), a real 3rd-century Chinese general later deified as a symbol of loyalty, integrity and justice, and worshipped in Chinese communities worldwide as a god of wealth and war.
interesting_fact: The pagoda has been enlarged and renovated several times, notably in 1895 and again in the early 2000s, but still houses a small library and historical artefacts documenting Chinese immigration to Mauritius - making it as much a community archive as a place of worship.

title: Kailassam Temple
about_site_text: Established in 1854, Kailassam Temple is recognised as the oldest Hindu temple in Mauritius, founded not long after the first waves of Indian indentured labourers began arriving at Aapravasi Ghat to work the island's sugar plantations. Dedicated to Shiva, it remains an active place of worship for Port Louis's Hindu community today.
interesting_fact: The temple's founding in 1854 places it squarely within the earliest years of Indian indentured migration to Mauritius, which began in 1834 - meaning it was built by, and for, some of the very first generation of Indo-Mauritians the Aapravasi Ghat site elsewhere on this tour was built to process.

title: St James Cathedral
address: St Denis St, Port Louis, Mauritius
about_site_text: The oldest Anglican church in Mauritius, consecrated as a cathedral on 26 June 1850. The building itself is older still and started life as "La Poudriere," a French colonial gunpowder magazine; after the British took control of the island the structure was converted for public use as a church from 1812, given an octagonal spire to make it look the part, and finally reopened for worship on Christmas Day 1831, before further wings were added in 1846 to fit its growing congregation.
interesting_fact: An appeal was launched in 2019 to fund urgent restoration of the historic building - a reminder that this centuries-old cathedral, built from a repurposed explosives store, is still a living, actively-used place of worship rather than a museum piece.

title: Institute of Contemporary Art Indian Ocean (ICAIO)
address: Sir Seewoosagur Ramgoolam St, Port Louis, Mauritius
about_site_text: A contemporary art gallery on Sir Seewoosagur Ramgoolam Street, set up in 2015 by Salim Currimjee, a Mauritian artist, photographer and architect, to give Indian Ocean-region artists a dedicated space for serious contemporary exhibitions rather than tourist-facing craft displays.
interesting_fact: ICAIO runs roughly four exhibitions a year, each lasting about three months, making it one of the few venues in Port Louis where the art on the walls actually changes throughout the year rather than being a permanent, static collection.

title: Didus Art Gallery
about_site_text: A gallery inside the Caudan Waterfront shopping centre that has spent more than twenty years showcasing painters, sculptors and craftspeople from across the Indian Ocean region, mixing contemporary work with more traditional Mauritian art.
interesting_fact: Its name nods to the dodo, Mauritius's extinct flightless bird and unofficial national mascot - a reminder that even a commercial gallery inside a shopping mall leans on the island's most famous piece of natural history for its branding.

title: House of Digital Art
address: Edith Cavell St, Port Louis, Mauritius
about_site_text: A gallery dedicated to digital and technology-driven art forms, blending traditional artistic expression with video, new media and interactive installations - a genuinely unusual offering on an island whose art scene is more often associated with painting and sculpture.
interesting_fact: Its presence in central Port Louis, alongside more traditional venues like Didus Art Gallery and ICAIO, reflects a growing contemporary-art scene in the capital that goes well beyond the postcard seascapes sold to tourists elsewhere on the island.

title: Line Barracks
address: Line Barracks St, Port Louis, Mauritius
about_site_text: A former colonial military barracks in the heart of Port Louis, later repurposed as a police headquarters, and formally listed by the Mauritius National Heritage Fund as a Scheduled Ancient Site. Barracks like this once housed the garrisons that controlled the island under both French and British rule, and the buildings' long institutional afterlife as a police compound has helped keep much of the original colonial-era structure intact.
interesting_fact: Line Barracks still functions as an operational police headquarters today, making it a rare case of a Port Louis heritage site that has never stopped being used for the purpose it was originally built for - military and civil order - across more than two centuries.

title: Trou Fanfaron
about_site_text: The stretch of Port Louis harbour where, from 1849, ships carrying indentured labourers from India actually docked and unloaded their passengers before they were processed at the neighbouring Aapravasi Ghat depot - clerks chalked numbers onto new arrivals' coats and doctors inspected them for scurvy right here on the wharf, before the first labourers were marched off within days to sugar estates across the island.
interesting_fact: "Trou Fanfaron" translates roughly as "braggart's hole" - an oddly jokey name for a site that was, in practice, the literal point of arrival for nearly half a million people during Mauritius's indentured-labour era.

title: Bourbon Street Food Vendors
address: Bourbon Street, near Central Market, Port Louis, Mauritius
about_site_text: A stretch of Bourbon Street, right by Port Louis Central Market, where some of the best-loved everyday Mauritian street food is sold each morning - dholl puri (soft split-pea flatbreads filled with spiced bean curry and rougaille sauce), crunchy gateaux piments (chilli-lentil fritters) and fresh alouda drinks, dished out from stalls locals queue for on their way to work.
interesting_fact: Dholl puri is so central to Mauritian daily life that it's often described as the island's unofficial national dish, despite being sold almost exclusively from unglamorous street stalls rather than restaurants - weekday mornings from around 7 to 10:30am are peak time to catch it fresh.

title: Jim Boulettes
about_site_text: A no-frills stall on Bourbon Street famous among Port Louis regulars for boulettes - small Chinese-Mauritian steamed or fried dumplings, sold cheap and fast, that count among the island's most popular grab-and-go snacks.
interesting_fact: Boulettes reflect Mauritius's 19th-century Chinese immigration just as directly as the pagodas and Chinatown gate elsewhere on this tour - descended from Cantonese dim sum traditions, they've become so thoroughly adopted into everyday Mauritian eating habits that most people no longer think of them as "Chinese food" at all.

title: Cafe L'Amicale
address: Emmanuel Anquetil St, Port Louis, Mauritius
about_site_text: A long-running Chinese-Mauritian restaurant near Port Louis's Chinatown gate, part of a small cluster of eateries - alongside Anam and Canton - that have served the Sino-Mauritian community's own comfort food for generations, rather than a westernised "Chinese restaurant" menu aimed at tourists.
interesting_fact: Its location just off the Chinatown arch makes it an easy stop for anyone exploring the historic Chinatown quarter, one Port Louis is proud to call one of the oldest outside China itself.

title: Lambic Beer Bar
address: St Georges St, Port Louis, Mauritius
about_site_text: A gastropub set inside a restored 19th-century colonial house on St Georges Street, popular for its wide range of Belgian and craft beers alongside Mauritian comfort food - an unusual pairing of European beer culture and Creole cooking in one of central Port Louis's older buildings.
interesting_fact: The building's colonial-era architecture is as much a draw as the beer list - it's one of a dwindling number of 19th-century townhouses in the capital that has been restored and kept in everyday public use rather than demolished for office towers.

title: Namaste Restaurant
about_site_text: A restaurant on the Caudan Waterfront overlooking Port Louis harbour, specialising in North Indian and Mughal-style dishes prepared by chefs trained in Delhi - a reflection of the deep, centuries-old links between Mauritius and the Indian subcontinent that run through much of this tour, from Aapravasi Ghat to the island's Hindu temples.
interesting_fact: Its harbour-view setting means diners can watch cargo ships and cruise liners come into port while eating a cuisine that first arrived on this same waterfront with indentured labourers nearly two centuries ago.
